summary: Is a positive integer equal to the sum of its proper positive divisors?
mainInsight: Enumerate divisor pairs up to sqrt(n): for each d with n % d == 0 add d and n // d (once if equal) and exclude n itself. Compare the sum with n. For n = 1 the answer is false because it has no proper divisors.

promptVariants: How do you enumerate the divisors of n efficiently?
Why can you stop at sqrt(n)?
options: Every divisor d <= sqrt(n) pairs with n // d >= sqrt(n)
Every divisor of n is at most n / 2 so check up to n / 2
Only the prime divisors matter so factorise first
cards.answer: Every divisor d <= sqrt(n) pairs with n // d >= sqrt(n)
cards.explanation: Collecting both members of the pair finds all divisors in O(sqrt n).

incorrectOptionExplanations.Only the prime divisors matter so factor: All divisors, not only primes, are summed.

promptVariants: What two special cases must be handled when summing divisor pairs?
cards.answer: n // d must be excluded when it equals n (that is not a proper divisor), and when d == n // d (a perfect square) it must be added only once. n = 1 has no proper divisors, so its divisor sum is 0 and it is not perfect.
keyPoints: Add a square root only once

cards.explanation: The loop runs up to sqrt(n).

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Space complexity (excluding the input): ___

options: No: the sum of its prime factors 2 + 7 = 9

incorrectOptionExplanations.No: 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 + 28 = 56: 28 itself is not a proper divisor.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Yes: 2 * 14 = 28 and 4 * 7 = 28: The divisors must be summed, not multiplied.
